The first lattice correction to Bloch's law
The spherical magnetization law for the three-dimensional quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet
Spontaneous magnetization in the quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet

headline: Proves 3D quantum Heisenberg ferromagnets magnetize at low temperature; claims Bloch's T^(3/2) law and its correction.
scope: The isotropic quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet on the cubic lattice and in dimensions three and up, at every spin and low positive temperature.
plain: A ferromagnet like iron stays magnetized with no outside field, below some temperature. For the standard quantum model of this, the Heisenberg ferromagnet, no one had proved that this ordering happens at any positive temperature. One paper shows it does in three or more dimensions, for every spin, and Lean checks this. Three more papers claim the exact low-temperature law for how magnetization falls, first found by Bloch in 1930, and its next correction.
doesNot: This does not cover one or two dimensions, where ordering is ruled out, or find the temperature where order disappears.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Felix Bloch, spin-wave prediction that magnetization falls like T^(3/2)
scorecard.significanceWhy: Spontaneous magnetization of the quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet at positive temperature is a long-standing open problem in mathematical physics.

explanation:
Picture a cubic grid with a tiny quantum magnet, a spin, at each point. Neighbouring spins lower their energy by lining up. At zero temperature all spins point the same way. Each spin-1/2 site then contributes its full value 1/2. Heat stirs up spin waves, ripples called magnons, and the average drops a little. Bloch predicted the drop is proportional to T^(3/2), where T is temperature[1]. Take spin S = 1/2 and β = 1/T = 20, so βS = 10. The predicted drop is ζ(3/2)/(8π^(3/2)) × 10^(−3/2), about 0.00185. Here ζ is the Riemann zeta function, with ζ(3/2) about 2.612. The magnetization is then about 0.4981 instead of 0.5.

That is a prediction. A proof must show order survives at a fixed positive temperature, with no outside field. The model, the Heisenberg ferromagnet, gives a quantum mechanism for ferromagnetism[2]. Its energy does not change if all spins rotate together. So a magnetized state must pick a direction on its own. That is spontaneous magnetization. In one and two dimensions, the Mermin–Wagner theorem rules it out[3]. In three dimensions, Dyson, Lieb and Simon proved ordering for the quantum antiferromagnet at spin one and up[4]. There, neighbours prefer to point opposite ways. Their method does not give the needed bound in the ferromagnetic case[5]. That gap was the obstacle.

The fourth paper settles existence. In every dimension d ≥ 3 and for every spin S, at low enough temperature there is an equilibrium state with magnetization at least S/4[6]. Equilibrium here means the KMS condition, the standard definition for infinite quantum systems. The paper says this resolves the low-temperature ordering problem in this formulation[7].

The other three papers claim exact laws in three dimensions. The first claims Bloch's T^(3/2) law at every spin[8]. Its coefficient comes from the spin-wave energy near zero momentum. The second claims the next term, 3ζ(5/2)(βS)^(−5/2)/(128π^(3/2))[9]. Dyson had traced this term to the grid shape of independent magnons[10]. In our example, βS = 10, it adds only about 0.0000179. The third claims that, on large cubes, the zero-field magnetization settles to a uniform direction with a fixed positive size[11].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, proves the existence result. For every d ≥ 3 and every spin, it builds the magnetized equilibrium state with magnetization at least S/4. Bloch's law, its correction and the spherical law are not in Lean. They rest on three long papers, and no specialist review of them has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. Spontaneous magnetization has a Lean proof; Bloch's law, its correction and the spherical law rest on unreviewed papers.

glossary.meaning: A grid of quantum spins where each neighbouring pair lowers its energy by pointing the same way.
The size of each quantum magnet: 1/2, 1, 3/2 and so on.
A net magnetization that survives with no outside magnetic field.
A spin wave: a ripple in the spin directions that carries a small unit of lost magnetization.
The prediction that magnetization falls below its maximum in proportion to T^(3/2) at low temperature.
The standard mathematical definition of a thermal equilibrium state for an infinite quantum system.
Inverse temperature, 1/T; large β means low temperature.

claims.text: Bloch predicted a magnetization deficit proportional to T^(3/2).

claims.sourceQuote: The spin-wave description of a ferromagnet begins with Bloch's prediction of a magnetization deficit proportional to \(T^{3/2}\), where \(T=\beta^{-1}\) \cite{Bloch1930}.

claims.sourceQuote: Dyson, Lieb and Simon proved quantum antiferromagnetic ordering for spin at least one in those dimensions, and for spin one half in sufficiently large dimension~\cite[Theorem~6.2]{DysonLiebSimon1978}.
